title: The case for organic assessment: 5 reasons to not outsource marking to AI
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Matthews argues that teachers should not outsource high-stakes summative marking to AI, using the Jurassic Park line about could versus should as his frame. He gives five reasons: assessment etymologically means sitting beside a learner, AI marking lowers the quality of student work by removing a human audience, it automates the wrong task when busywork is the better target, hand marking is professional development, and it informs in-the-moment teaching. He is explicit that routine retrieval quizzes are outside his claim and lists tasks AI can legitimately take over. The piece is personal and anecdotal rather than evidence-heavy, but it gives a coherent school-level position on a live AI policy question and fits the author's established Ed-Tech output.
points: Capability is not obligation: the author separates what AI could mark from what teachers should leave to humans.
Students write better for human audiences, so algorithmic grading risks degrading the work itself.
AI should take over busywork such as simplified texts, sentence stems and exemplars, freeing time for assessment.
Marking by hand shows what stuck from teaching and supplies the knowledge of learners that makes targeted in-class feedback possible.
quotes: With AI moving at the speed of a bullet out of a gun, we could do all sorts of things. We could automate, outsource, and delegate large chunks of our life and work.

When we outsource our assessment to AI, we are leaving the metaphorical table and politely ushering a robot into our seat. We vacate the seat beside our learner and, in doing so, contort the very thing we’re doing.
Audience matters. How we do our work is shaped by who we are doing our work for.
AI can help us speed up the busywork so we can spend more time on the things that shouldn’t be rushed. And assessment is one of the things that shouldn’t be rushed.
And the simple truth is that assessment doesn’t just give us feedback on student learning. It gives us feedback on our teaching.
As I read multiple assessments I get a feel for what got absorbed and what didn’t - what needs more oxygen and what can afford to have less air-time.
But because I already had the data points in mind, I was able to look for it, spot it, and give some quick, targeted advice.
